title: Paper 2 Question 5: arguing a point of view
specPoints: Paper 2 Section B: Question 5, writing to present a viewpoint (AO5 24 marks, AO6 16 marks)

tips.title: Issue, form, audience, purpose
tips.body: Read all four off the task before planning. The statement gives the issue; the specification promises the form, the audience and the purpose every time. Each decides something: the argument, the conventions, the register, the shape.

tips.title: Position first
tips.body: State a view in the first paragraph, ideally in a picture the reader can see. A both-sides shrug or an announcement of intent is not an opening; it is a delay.

tips.title: The counter-argument is the test
tips.body: State the objection fairly, grant what is true in it, answer it, and keep the same voice while you do. Most pieces lose their register there, and it is the paragraph that makes an argument complex.

tips.title: One of each, placed
tips.body: One triplet where the argument gathers, one question the reader will answer your way, one person in three sentences, one figure you can stand behind, one concession. Placed, not sprinkled.

tips.title: For the reader, not the examiner
tips.body: The task names who is reading. Write to them: you or we for a magazine, a title for a head teacher, a room for a speech. The examiner is reading over their shoulder.

tips.title: Links that move
tips.body: It will be said that. And there is a second reason. Which brings the question back to. These carry an argument; furthermore and in addition bolt paragraphs on and move nothing.

why.matters: Arguing a point of view in writing is the skill by which most things are decided: a letter that changes a rule, an article that changes a mind, a speech that carries a room. The exam gives it forty marks and names the reader every time, because persuasion is not a set of tricks but a relationship: a position stated, reasons a reader can follow, the objection met in the reader's hearing, and a voice the reader trusts because it is held. The student who can do that on a Tuesday afternoon about homework can do it in the letters and meetings where it counts, and can also recognise it when it is being done to them.

examples.title: The letter that gets an answer
examples.body: A complaint to a company, a request to a council, a case made to a head teacher: the ones that work state what they want in the first paragraph, give two reasons the reader can check, meet the reason the reader will have for saying no, and keep a courteous voice throughout. The five-line plan is the shape of every letter that has ever changed something.

examples.title: Being persuaded on purpose
examples.body: An advertisement, a campaign, a speech at a rally: each uses the triplet, the question, the anecdote and the figure, and each hopes the reader will not notice. The writer who has placed those devices with intent in their own argument can see them placed in someone else's, and can decide whether to be moved before being moved. Writing to argue is also the reading skill that no source-based question teaches.

steps.title: Question 5: a statement, a form, an audience
steps.body:
Paper 2 Section B is one task worth forty marks, the same as Paper 1's, and it always has the same shape: a statement in quotation marks, then an instruction naming a form and an audience and a purpose. June 2024: *Choosing a future career should be based on helping others and making a positive contribution to society, not achieving status or making lots of money.* Write an article for your school or college magazine in which you argue your point of view on this statement.

**Three things to read off the task.** The issue, in the statement. The form: an article, a letter, a speech, sometimes an essay or a leaflet. The audience and purpose: a school magazine, to argue; a newspaper, to explain; a head teacher, to persuade. The specification says the task will specify audience, purpose and form and use statements, opinions and scenarios to provoke a response, on the theme of Section A.

**The same two ladders.** Twenty-four marks for content and organisation, sixteen for technical accuracy, marked as on Paper 1. The descriptors do not change; what changes is that the register is matched to a real form and a named audience, and the ideas are an argument.

**Time.** About 45 minutes: five to plan, thirty-five to write, five to check.

steps.title: The shape of an argument
steps.body:
An argument has a position, reasons, an opponent, and an ending that asks something of the reader. The plan is five lines.

**A position, stated early.** Not *this is a difficult question with two sides*, but a view: *a career should be chosen for the good it does, and the money will follow or it will not matter*. The descriptors reward convincing communication, and conviction begins with a position.

**Two or three reasons, each developed.** A reason is a paragraph: the claim, a case that shows it, what follows from it. Three reasons in one paragraph are a list; one reason in a paragraph is an argument.

**The counter-argument, met.** *It will be said that nobody can eat good intentions.* Then the answer. An argument that never meets its opponent is a speech to the converted, and the top band asks for complex ideas.

**An ending that asks.** A call to the reader, a return to the opening, a question left in the air: the last paragraph is where the register is judged.

**Ideas that are the writer's own.** The task in June 2024 followed two sources about medicine. Use them as evidence if they help, but the argument is yours, and the ideas the descriptors call compelling are the ones a reader has not heard before.

visuals.alt: A flow chart of the shape of an argument: a position stated early, two reasons developed, the counter-argument met, and an ending that asks something of the reader

check.prompt: Why does an argument need to meet its counter-argument?
check.solution: Meeting the objection is where an argument becomes convincing: it shows the writer has thought, and it gives the reader a reason to agree rather than an instruction to. One paragraph, the objection stated fairly and then answered, is enough.

markScheme.description: Because an argument that never faces its opponent is a speech to the converted

Because the examiners deduct marks from any answer with fewer than four paragraphs, and the counter-argument makes the fourth
Because the counter-argument is always the correct view and must be adopted
Because a counter-argument makes the piece longer

steps.title: Register: who is being spoken to, and how
steps.body:
The top AO5 descriptor is tone, style and register assuredly matched to purpose and audience, and in Question 5 the audience is named. A school magazine is read by students and teachers; a broadsheet by adults who expect to be reasoned with; a head teacher by one person with the power to say no.

**What changes with the audience.** The vocabulary, how much is assumed, how much humour, whether the reader is *you* or *we* or *the reader*. A magazine article can be wry and quick; a letter to a head teacher is courteous and specific; a speech to a year group is direct and spoken.

**What never changes.** Standard English in the narration of the argument, sentence forms varied on purpose, and a register held from the first line to the last. A piece that opens with a joke and ends with a sermon has not been controlled.

**The trap.** Writing for the examiner. The task names a reader; the piece is for them, and the examiner is reading over their shoulder.

steps.title: Devices with intent
steps.body:
Rhetoric is the craft of making a reader agree, and its devices earn marks when they are placed to do something and lose them when they are sprinkled.

**The triplet.** Three parallel items, the third longest: *a job that pays the rent, a job that fills the day, a job that is worth the life spent on it.*

**The rhetorical question, once.** Placed where the reader is ready to answer it the writer's way. Three in a paragraph are a tic.

**The anecdote.** One person, one moment, told in three sentences, that makes the abstract concrete. A nurse who chose the ward over the bank, and what she said about it.

**The figure you can stand behind.** A statistic invented on the spot is noticed; a plain, believable observation is not. *Most of the people who taught me will never be rich* beats *87% of teachers are underpaid*.

**The concession.** *It is true that …* followed by *but*. The device that makes an argument sound fair.

**The short sentence.** After the long one, at the turn. As in every kind of writing.

steps.title: Organisation: paragraphs that argue
steps.body:
The organisation half of AO5 asks for structural features used with intent, and for paragraphs fluently linked with discourse markers seamlessly integrated. In an argument, the structure is the argument.

**Each paragraph one move.** Position; reason; reason; counter met; ending. The first sentence of each paragraph says what the paragraph is for.

**Links that argue.** *And there is a second reason. It will be said that. Which brings the question back to.* These carry the argument forward; *furthermore* and *in addition* bolt paragraphs together without moving anything.

**A structure the reader feels.** A return to the opening in the last paragraph. A question posed early and answered late. A concession placed just before the strongest reason, so the reason lands on the objection.

**The title, if the form has one.** An article's headline is part of the register: short, and promising the argument.

Think about who you remember, and why
And there is a second reason: status is lent
It will be said that ideals do not pay rent
So: Mr Adeyemi. What did he choose?

steps.title: Five lines on a statement
steps.body:
Take this statement: *Homework should be abolished, because it does more harm than good.* Write a speech to your year group arguing your point of view. Plan in five lines: position; reason one; reason two; the counter, met; the ending. Then write the opening paragraph and the counter-argument paragraph, in ten minutes.

Check the register: is it spoken, direct, for a room of people your age? Is the position in the first paragraph? Does the counter-argument state the objection fairly before answering it?

steps.title: Compelling: an argument the reader has not heard
steps.body:
Upper Level 4 asks for compelling, complex ideas, tone assuredly matched, sustained crafting, inventive structure. In viewpoint writing each has a particular meaning.

**Complex.** Not more reasons but a reason with a turn in it: the money runs out of things to buy; status is lent and can be recalled. An idea the reader has to think about is complex; a list of obvious reasons is not.

**Assured.** The register chosen for the named audience and held, including through the counter-argument, where most pieces turn earnest and lose their voice.

**Sustained.** One image or case, Mr Adeyemi, carried from the opening to the ending, rather than a new device in every paragraph.

**Inventive.** A structure the reader feels: the question answered late, the concession placed under the strongest reason, the return.

**And accurate.** Sixteen marks, the same five minutes. Argument tempts long sentences; check that each has one main clause and that the semicolons are joining sentences.

steps.title: Arguing a point of view in one page
steps.body:
Forty marks, forty-five minutes, one argument for a named reader.

- **Read the task:** the issue in the statement; the form; the audience; the purpose. The specification names all three every time.
- **The shape:** a position stated early; two or three reasons, each a paragraph; the counter-argument met; an ending that asks.
- **Register:** matched to the named audience and held to the last line; written for the reader, not the examiner.
- **Devices with intent:** one triplet, one question, one anecdote, a figure you can stand behind, a concession; never sprinkled.
- **Organisation that argues:** each paragraph one move, links that move the argument, a structure the reader feels.
- **Compelling:** a reason with a turn in it; one case carried through; five minutes to check.

The forms, article, letter, speech, have their own topic.

Check demarcation, semicolons, spelling; make sure the ending asks

questions.prompt: Write the opening two paragraphs of the June 2024 article: a school or college magazine, arguing your point of view on the statement that a career should be chosen for helping others rather than status or money. State a position in the first paragraph in a case the reader can picture; develop one reason in the second. Hold a register for students throughout.
questions.solution:
Nobody remembers who had the biggest car in the year above. Everybody remembers Mr Adeyemi. He taught us Year 8 science in a lab that smelt of gas and biscuits, he never once raised his voice, and he is the reason four people in my year want to be doctors. He is not, as far as I know, rich. I am not sure he would know what to do with it if he were.

That is the first reason for choosing a career by the good it does rather than the money it makes: think about who you actually remember. Not the people with the status, because status is a thing other people hand you and can take back, and by the time you are old enough to notice it, they usually have. The people you remember are the ones who did something for you when they did not have to. Teachers, mostly. A nurse, if you were unlucky enough to need one. The man who fixed the bike. None of them were paid for being remembered. All of them were, and are, and will be.

questions.prompt: Write a complete speech of about 500 words to your year group arguing your point of view on this statement: Homework should be abolished, because it does more harm than good. Plan first: position, two reasons, the counter-argument met, an ending that asks. Write for a room, in a register you hold to the last line.
questions.solution:
Put your hands up if you did all of last night's homework. Keep them up if you did it well. Now keep them up if you learned something from it that you did not know at four o'clock. I will not turn round; I already know what the room looks like.

I am going to argue that homework should go, and I want to be precise about what I mean, because the other side will not be. I do not mean that we should never work at home. I mean that the nightly ration, set because it is Tuesday and Tuesday is science, should stop, because it does more harm than the good it is meant to do.

Here is the first harm. Three hours a night teaches most of us to work badly. It teaches us to start at nine, to copy, to finish, to hand in. Nobody in this room learned to think in the third hour of a Tuesday. The people who did learn to work alone, and some did, would have learned it in one hour that they had chosen, on something they cared about.

Here is the second. Homework is the great leveller in reverse. If you have a desk, a quiet room and a parent who did the subject, it is a small thing. It is exactly true. And it is an argument for practice that we choose, that we are taught how to do, and that is judged by what we learned rather than by whether it was in on Wednesday. criteria.text: The position is stated in the first paragraph and the piece has the shape of an argument: two reasons developed, a counter-argument met, an ending that asks
The register is a speech to a year group, spoken and direct, and is held throughout, including through the counter-argument
Devices are used with intent: a triplet, a question, an anecdote or a figure the speaker can stand behind, a concession
The writing is accurate: sentences demarcated, punctuation varied and correct, spelling secure

questions.modelAnswer:
Put your hands up if you did all of last night's homework. Keep them up if you did it well. Now keep them up if you learned something from it that you did not know at four o'clock. I will not turn round; I already know what the room looks like.

I am going to argue that homework should go, and I want to be precise about what I mean, because the other side will not be. I do not mean that we should never work at home. I mean that the nightly ration, set because it is Tuesday and Tuesday is science, should stop, because it does more harm than the good it is meant to do.

Here is the first harm. Three hours a night teaches most of us to work badly. It teaches us to start at nine, to copy, to finish, to hand in. questions.prompt: A student's article is lively and well argued but loses its voice in the counter-argument paragraph, which reads like an essay. What does the examiner see?
questions.solution: The register is judged across the piece, and the counter-argument is the test of it: an objection can be met in the same voice that made the case. A change of voice there is control slipping, not a device.

markScheme.description: A register not sustained: assuredly matched means held through the whole piece, and the counter-argument is where most lose it

options: A problem with accuracy, since essays and articles are punctuated differently
A register not sustained: assuredly matched means held through the whole piece, and the counter-argument is where most lose it
Nothing: the counter-argument is supposed to be written in a different register from the rest, so that the reader can tell which side is speaking
A structural feature used with intent, since the change of voice marks the change of side

questions.prompt: A student says: 'The more persuasive devices I use, the higher the mark.' What is the better account?
questions.solution: The descriptors reward crafting sustained across a piece, not a count of techniques. A device used once where it does something is craft; the same device three times a paragraph is a tic that tells the examiner the writer is performing persuasion rather than persuading.

markScheme.description: Devices earn when placed with intent and cost when sprinkled: one triplet, one question, one case carried through, and a register that does not sound like a checklist

options: The student is right, and a device in every sentence is the aim, since the examiners count them and award a mark for each one they find
Devices earn nothing at all, and the argument should be plain throughout, because the examiners are marking the ideas and not the way they are expressed
Devices earn when placed with intent and cost when sprinkled: one triplet, one question, one case carried through, and a register that does not sound like a checklist
Only rhetorical questions earn marks in an argument, so use as many as possible and put one at the end of every paragraph

examTechnique.body:
**Read the task for four things:** the issue in the statement, the form, the audience, the purpose. The specification names the last three every time.

**Plan in five lines:** a position; two reasons, each a paragraph; the counter-argument, met; an ending that asks. About 45 minutes: five to plan, thirty-five to write, five to check.

**Register for the named reader,** held to the last line and through the counter-argument. Standard English in the argument's own voice.

**Devices with intent, one of each.** A figure you can stand behind, never an invented percentage.

**Organisation that argues:** each paragraph one move, links that move the argument, a return or a question at the end.

**Sixteen marks for accuracy,** on the same scale as Paper 1: argument tempts long sentences, so check the demarcation.
examinerErrors: Opening with a both-sides shrug or an announcement of intent instead of a position.
Writing for the examiner rather than the reader the task names, so the register is nobody's.
Sprinkling devices, three rhetorical questions in a paragraph, a triplet in every sentence, an invented statistic.
Dismissing the counter-argument in a clause, or never meeting it at all.
Losing the voice in the counter-argument paragraph and finishing as an essay.
Bolting paragraphs together with furthermore and in addition, and ending with in conclusion.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 argument knows who it is talking to and never forgets: the register is the named audience's from the first line, it is held through the counter-argument, and the reader is addressed as the form addresses them. It opens on a position in a picture, gives two reasons with a turn in each, meets the objection fairly and answers it in the same voice, and ends by returning to the opening or asking the reader something. Its devices are few and placed; its figures are believable; its paragraphs each make one move and are linked by sentences that argue; and its sentences are demarcated, because five minutes were kept.
